content: 1. Step 3 of the CARE 20 Planning process focuses on determining the methods to achieve the goals of palliative care. This includes bridging gaps in palliative care services, raising necessary resources, and organizing cancer palliative care services across all levels of care. 2. A team-based approach should be adopted, with a clear understanding of the roles of healthcare providers. Palliative care teams should be created to address the multifaceted needs of patients and their families. 3. Caregivers should be educated to provide effective support, and public awareness campaigns should be conducted to educate the general public and policymakers about the importance of palliative care. 4. It is essential to ensure the availability of essential medications, particularly for pain management and symptom control, including opioids for effective pain relief. 5. Palliative care standards should be developed, and the implementation of palliative care plans and activities should be regularly evaluated and monitored to ensure effectiveness. 6. Palliative care is a critical humanitarian need worldwide, especially for individuals with cancer and other chronic, life-threatening illnesses. It is particularly vital in regions where patients often present in advanced stages of disease with limited chances of cure. 7. Ideally, palliative care services should begin at the time of diagnosis of a life-threatening illness and adapt to the increasing needs of patients and their families as the disease progresses to the terminal phase. These services should also provide bereavement support to families. 8. Effective palliative care services are integrated into existing healthcare systems at all levels, particularly in community and home-based care settings. They involve both public and private sectors and are tailored to the specific cultural, social, and economic contexts of the population. 9. Palliative care services should be strategically linked to cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment services to maximize the use of limited resources and address the priority needs of cancer patients in the community. 10. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), palliative care improves the quality of life for patients and their families facing life-threatening illnesses. It achieves this through the prevention and relief of suffering, early identification, and impeccable assessment and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial, and spiritual problems. 11. Palliative care provides relief from pain and distressing symptoms, affirms life while recognizing dying as a natural process, and neither hastens nor postpones death. It integrates psychological and spiritual aspects of care and supports patients to live as actively as possible until death. 12. Palliative care also offers a support system to help families cope during the patient’s illness and in their bereavement. It uses a team approach to address the needs of patients and families, including bereavement counseling if needed. 13. Palliative care enhances the quality of life and may positively influence the course of illness. It is applicable early in the course of illness, alongside therapies intended to prolong life, such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy. 14. Terminal cancer refers to an advanced stage of the disease where curative treatment is no longer effective, the condition is deemed incurable, and the patient’s health is progressively deteriorating. 15. Palliative care is concerned not only with addressing all aspects of the patient’s needs but also with the needs of their families and healthcare providers. It is a key component of comprehensive cancer control programs and broader palliative care strategies. 16. A public health approach to palliative care is essential in all countries to address the needs of advanced cancer patients and their families, ensuring universal access to necessary services at all levels of care within the health system. 17. Three foundational measures are required for developing palliative care with a public health approach: a government policy to integrate palliative care into the national healthcare system, an educational policy to train healthcare professionals and the public, and a drug policy to ensure the availability of essential medications for pain and symptom management. 18. Effective palliative care planning involves assessing the specific needs of patients, healthcare providers, and family caregivers. This includes organizing services to meet those needs and ensuring accessible and affordable medications for symptom management. 19. The planning process should also evaluate the existing palliative care plan and activities, ensuring they are part of a comprehensive cancer control program and integrated with other related health activities. 20. The ultimate goal of palliative care is to relieve suffering, improve the quality of life for patients and their families, and provide support throughout the illness and bereavement phases.
